# Research

## Job Market Paper

### Landowner Expectations of Wildfire Risk have Accelerated Harvest and Reduced Volume in Western U.S. Forests
*with Christopher Mihiar and David J. Lewis*

*Abstract.* Wildfire risk has intensified across the western United States, generating hundreds of billions of dollars in economic damages each year. Economic theory shows that changing wildfire risk should induce landowners to reduce risk exposure through forest management, though there is little empirical evidence of such landowner adaptation. This study provides the first large-scale empirical evidence on how increasing wildfire risk affects plot-level forest management decisions on non-federal land. Using confidential plot-level data from the U.S.D.A. Forest Service Forest Inventory and Analysis program linked with wildfire perimeters and fire-related weather conditions, we examine how nearby wildfires and hotter, drier fire seasons influence the choice among harvest types and decisions regarding planting density on private and state timberland in Oregon, California, and Washington. Controlling for plot and climate factors, we find that increased wildfire exposure and a warmer, drier climate lead landowners to harvest more and to lower their planting densities, revealing adaptive responses to changing fire risk consistent with predictions from natural resource economic theory. A bio-economic simulation shows that the changing fire regime since 2001 has reduced standing volume in non-federal western forests by roughly 7 to 10 percent. We quantify two of the externalities this creates. Holding observed fires fixed, adaptation raised PM2.5 emissions from the 2020 fire season by about 0.3 percent but lowered CO2 emissions by 0.4 to 0.9 percent, driven by changes in surface fuels and crown fuels. We value the resulting smoke damages at \$63 to \$72 million, which outweigh climate benefits of \$28 to \$58 million.
